Bhīṣmaparva
------------------------------------------
This is the sixth book of the gigantic epic Mahābhārata, of which the celebrated Bhagavadgītā is an integral part. Exploits of the invincible भीष्म, the grand-sire of the कुरु race and his lying on the deathbed of arrows after laying down his arms are the chief contents of this book.
See MAHĀBHĀRATA.

Bhīṣma
(‘the terrible’)
------------------------------------------
The Mahābhārata, the bigger of the two epics of हिन्दुइस्म् and the greatest didactic poem of the world, has held up before us many a hero fit to be emulated if not adored. And, भीष्म, the grand-sire of the Kaurava race, is pre-eminent among them. Ranked as next only to कृष्ण, considered as God-incarnate, भीष्म was not only the greatest of the warriors of his times, he was also a towering intellect and a paragon of virtues.
Originally a Vasu (one of the eight attendants of इन्द्र) he was born, due to a curse, as the eighth son of the king Śantanu in गङ्गा, the river goddess. गङ्गा christened him as ‘Devavrata,’ brought him up well, got him well-educated and trained under the warrior-sage परशुराम and then handed him back to the king Śantanu. The king took him to his capital, हस्तिनापुर, and made him the Yuvarāja or the crown-prince.
One day, Śantanu who had gone out hunting, fell in love with सत्यवती, the daughter of the chieftain of the fishermen. When he proposed to marry her, the chieftain laid the condition that the son that would be born in her should be the heir to the throne. The king obviously could not concede the demand as it would be a great injustice to देवव्रत, who was the fittest heir anointed to be so. However, the lovelorn king could neither forget the girl nor consent to the condition laid by her ड़थेर्. This conflict had a devastating effect on him. When देवव्रत noticed it and learnt of the details, he went to the chieftain, vowed before him that he would willingly abdicate his right over the kingdom, nor would he ever marry so that his progeny could never stake its claim over it. This terrible vow earned him the name ‘Bhīṣma,’ ‘the terrible’ which stuck.
Śantanu married सत्यवती and begot two sons—Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya. Both of them died without issues. Then, at the request of सत्यवती and as per the ‘niyoga’ custom (See NIYOGA for details.) that was prevalent during those days, sage व्यास raised issues in अम्बिका and Ambālikā the queens of Vicitravīrya. The two sons were named धृतराष्ट्र and पाण्डु. The former was born blind.
Bhīṣma brought them up, got them married and, they in course of time, had their own children: the hundred Kauravas and the five Pāṇḍavas. दुर्योधन and दुश्शासन were the first two among the Kauravas. The Pāṇḍvas were: युधिष्ठिर, भीम, अर्जुन, नकुल and सहदेव.
There was constant rivalry between these two groups of cousins, दुर्योधन being the villain while युधिष्ठिर was the paragon of धर्म or righteousness. दुर्योधन made several attempts to decimate the Pāṇḍavas, but destiny always sided with the latter. भीष्म had quite a tough time in forging a working alliance between them and his sage counsels often had their effect and prevented many a crisis.
After the मर्रिअगे of the Pāṇḍavas with द्रौपदी, भीष्म was instrumental in recalling them from their self-imposed exile and returning them their share of the kingdom. The Pāṇḍavas built a beauti-ful capital city and named it इन्द्रप्रस्थ. However, दुर्योधन succeeded in usurping their kingdom by jealous machinations and insulted द्रौपदी, the Pāṇḍava queen, in the open assembly. But their kingdom and wealth were restored to them by the intervention of the blind king धृतराष्ट्र.
This truce was however shortlived. In a subsequent game of dice, युधिष्ठिर lost everything and when the Pāṇḍavas later demanded their kingdom back, as per the agreement, दुर्योधन refused it, resulting in the well-known कुरुक्षेत्र war. भीष्म was the first commander-in-chief of the Kaurava army. Though he fought valiantly he was ultimately downed by अर्जुन. Since he had the special boon of dying at will, he chose to live on—though badly wounded—for a period of 58 days, till the उत्तरायण or the period of the northern solstice. At the behest of कृष्ण, भीष्म gave a long discourse on the various aspects of धर्म in answer to the questions raised by युधिष्ठिर. This section of the Mahā-bhārata known as the Śāntiparva is an invaluable source of धर्म even now. He then gave up the body in योग.
See also MAHĀBHĀRATA.
